title: Another self
hook: Aristotle: a friend is another self (Nicomachean Ethics 9.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aristotle's three friendships. Your line was friends of the good. Did you do one small thing for a friend's sake? Today, Aristotle goes a step further, in two Greek words. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

Good news arrives, and some people's thumbs go straight to one particular name. Bad news, the same name. Nobody decided that on purpose; it just grew. In the ninth book of his Ethics, Aristotle looks at that kind of bond and asks an odd question. Where does it come from? His answer starts somewhere unexpected: not with the friend at all, but with how a good person lives with themself.
screen: `ONE NAME FOR GOOD NEWS.` → `AN ODD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the marks of a friend. Aristotle lists what people take friendship to mean: wishing good to someone for their sake, wishing them to exist and to live, spending time with them, choosing the same things, sharing their griefs and their joys. Second, it starts at home. Then he turns the list around. A good person, he says, already relates to themself this way: wants their own good, wants to go on living, is glad of their own company, and isn't at war inside. Third, another self. And so, he says, the good person is to a friend as to themself, for a friend is another self. In Greek that's two words, allos autos. The friend isn't a copy. The friend is someone whose good matters to you the way your own does, whose griefs land on you as if they were yours. Fourth, the warning inside. Aristotle turns then to bad people, and draws them as the opposite: at odds with themselves, running from their own company, full of regret for what they've chosen, with no friendly feeling even toward themselves. Some readers take a hopeful thought from the passage: peace inside and friendship outside may grow from the same root, and tending one may help the other.
screen: `THE MARKS OF A FRIEND.` · `IT STARTS AT HOME.` · `ALLOS AUTOS, ANOTHER SELF.` · `THE WARNING INSIDE.` · then, large: `ANOTHER SELF.`

segments.voice: Bring one friend to mind. Breathe in, and wish them what you'd wish yourself today: rest, a good meal, an easy hour, some good news. Breathe out, and if it isn't too hard, wish yourself the same. Go back and forth for a while, friend and self, self and friend, until the two wishes start to sound alike. If one wish comes easily and the other is hard, just notice which one, without judging it. The bell holds the time.
Another self. Aristotle's phrase, allos autos: a friend is someone whose good matters to you the way your own does. Today's word.
Your line: another self. Today, before you reply to a friend, ask how you'd want to be answered, and answer that way. Day eight hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Aristotle's idea of the friend as another self, from book nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, is studied in philosophy courses, and some readers use it to reflect on how they treat friends and themselves.

match.prompt: Aristotle on friendship — tap the pairs.

myth: Aristotle means a friend should be a copy of you
another self means someone whose good matters to you like your own.
sharing griefs and joys is on Aristotle's list of friendship's marks
along with wishing their good and spending time together.
Aristotle says how you live with yourself has nothing to do with friendship
he starts with a good person's relation to themself.

fork.setup: you're Aristotle, explaining where friendship comes from. where do you look first?
options: at how a good person relates to themself.
at what a friend can do for you.
at how many friends a person has.
fork.reveal: he looks inward first: a good person already wishes their own good and enjoys their own company, and is to a friend as to themself.

original.note: Greek: another self, Aristotle's phrase for a friend.

trapdoor: what you thought: another self means someone just like you.
what it means: a friend is someone you relate to as to yourself: wishing their good, sharing their joys and griefs.
what a scholar hears: Aristotle models friendship on a good person's relation to themself, so peace inside and friendship outside are linked.

notes: Aristotle paraphrased (no translation on the validator's public-domain list).
List of friendship's marks and the good man's relation to himself follow 9.4 (1166a); 'a friend is another self' (allos autos) at 1166a31–32. Confirm the Greek phrase and pronunciation.
The bad man's division against himself and flight from his own company at 1166b; 'even to themselves' compresses his point; confirm.

Audit: the fourth teach section said Aristotle's warning was about 'people who are at odds with themselves' who 'find it hard to be friends to anyone'. In 9.4 (1166b) he is describing bad (phauloi) people, and says they lack friendly feeling toward themselves; the 'to anyone' was not in the text. Rewritten to attribute the picture to bad people as Aristotle draws them, and the narrator's 'read gently, it's a hopeful thought' now credited to 'some readers'. Match pair adjusted. Carry ('answer as you'd want to be answered') kept; day 825's carry changed so the golden-rule phrasing isn't repeated.
Editor: cut the practice's closing 'do one thing for that friend' line, which repeated yesterday's carry (one small thing for a friend's sake).
